_schema: CERTIFIED HARDWARE DATA. This file is the source of truth for https://screentinker.com/certified-hardware.
The page is GENERATED from this file. Edit here, never in frontend/certified-hardware.html.
Then run:  cd server && npm run build:certified-hardware
A test fails if the committed HTML does not match this file, so a forgotten rebuild cannot ship.
WHY THIS IS NOT AN ORDINARY MARKETING PAGE: reseller agreements define 'Certified Hardware' as the
models published here, and support obligations attach to what appears on this list. Nothing gets
status 'certified' or 'certified-with-limits' unless ScreenTinker actually tested it and retains a
unit. If you do not know a value, leave it null. Never guess a model number, version or date.
FIELDS (every one is required; use null for unknown, never omit the key):
id             url-safe slug, STABLE FOREVER. It is the deep-link anchor (#fire-tv-stick-4k-max)
and resellers paste those links into quotes. Renaming one breaks their documents.
name           full product name as sold
manufacturer   brand, or null where there is none (the web player, white-label hardware)
model_numbers  array of the SKUs this entry actually covers, or null. One entry may cover several.
category       streaming-player | soc-display | media-player | browser | sbc
os             OS family and the specific version tested
player         which ScreenTinker player build runs on it
status         see STATUS below
max_resolution what it actually does, not what the box claims
validated_on   ISO date (YYYY-MM-DD) of the test. In practice this is usually the day the tested
build was released, because testing happens at release time.
validated_by   'ScreenTinker' or 'Community'
player_version ScreenTinker version it was tested against. Where an entry has a min_version and
no player_version, they are the same: the floor was set by the test that
established it.
min_version    minimum ScreenTinker version for this status to hold, or null if it always held.
POLICY: min_version is a FLOOR, and it is STICKY. It starts as the version
tested when the device was first certified and then stays put. Retesting on a
newer build raises player_version and leaves min_version alone, because the
older floor still held on the day it was tested. It goes UP, never DOWN:
raise it when you learn older builds no longer qualify, and never lower it to a
version nobody tested. Invariant, enforced by a test: min_version is never
newer than player_version — you cannot require more than you have tested.
0.0.1 is meaningful and is not a placeholder: it means this has worked since the
very first release and has no floor. Do not 'tidy' it to null — null renders as
"Not recorded", which says the opposite of what is true.
provisioning_url  link to the setup guide for this device, or null
buy_url        affiliate / where-to-buy link (https URL) shown as a "Buy this device" link,
or null. Marked rel=sponsored nofollow and disclosed as affiliate on the page.
notes          array of short strings: gotchas, limitations, required settings
eol            manufacturer end-of-life date if announced, else null
STATUS:
certified             ScreenTinker tested it, it works, supported under agreements, unit kept in lab
certified-with-limits supported WITH a documented limitation. The limitation MUST be in notes.
community-reported    a user says it works. NOT tested by ScreenTinker. NOT Certified Hardware.
known-issues          it runs but something is broken. Say what, in notes.
not-supported         tested, does not work well enough to recommend. Say why, in notes,
because people will otherwise buy it anyway.
Order within a status group is the order of this array. Groups are ordered by the list above.

devices.name: Amazon Fire TV Stick 4K Max
notes: The primary recommendation for a new installation.
Validated at 1920x1080. The device supports higher output, but 4K signage playback has not been validated and is not covered.
Drives a commercial display over HDMI. The display itself needs no certification.

devices.name: BrightSign Series 5
devices.player: Web player, running in an roHtmlWidget under the BrightSign autorun package (autorun.zip: autorun.brs plus st-bridge.js)
notes: The player code is the ordinary web player, unmodified. The BrightSign-specific part is the host around it: autorun.brs owns the widget lifecycle, identity across reboots, recovery from a dead server, and video-mode and multi-output control, with st-bridge.js as the page's half of that contract. This package has to be installed on the player.

BrightSign's HTML widget does not reliably come back from a page reload. That is why the host exists: on deploy the page asks for a restart and autorun.brs tears the widget down and builds a new one, which is a restart the operating system actually performs. Without that host a deploy can darken the panel until someone power-cycles it.
The same hardware can also run the ScreenTinker server itself rather than only the player. That is a separate configuration with its own requirements, listed below.

devices.name: BrightSign Series 5, running the ScreenTinker server
devices.player: The ScreenTinker server itself, as a real Node process, with the player running in the widget beside it
notes: This is the whole system on one box: no separate server to host, and the panel keeps working if the network does not.
BrightSign OS 10 is required, and is not optional. The server runs on the Node runtime that ships with OS 10. OS 9 can run the player but cannot run the server.

NVMe or SSD storage is REQUIRED. Do not run the server from an SD card. A server writes continuously, to its database, its write-ahead log, its media library and its logs, and that load will wear out an SD card and take the site down with it. This is why the entry names the XT245, which takes a 128 GB NVMe drive, rather than the Series 5 generally.
Server mode is off unless you ask for it. It listens on port 8181.

Install from the autorun-server.zip and server-payload.zip assets published with each release. The payload installs in two stages; a single combined archive is not usable because the boot-time archive reader does not handle one that large.
Newer than the player configuration, which has been running since 2026-08-07. Treat it accordingly.

devices.name: KB1001 Android tablet
notes: The panel is 1280x800. It was tested with 1080p content, which the device downscales to fit, so a 1080p playlist plays correctly but is not shown at full resolution.

Requires ScreenTinker 1.9.4 or later. Earlier Android builds could strand a panel on "waiting for content" after a restart, with no recovery short of clearing the app and re-provisioning (issue #162, fixed 2026-07-10).

devices.name: Web player (any browser)
devices.os: Any operating system with a current browser
notes: Tested on Chrome and Firefox. Edge is expected to work but has not been tested.
Point the browser at /player on your server. Nothing is installed.
No minimum browser version has been established.
There is no ScreenTinker version floor either. The browser has been a supported display since the first release, and it is re-tested with the current one.

devices.name: Samsung OM55B
notes: ScreenTinker holds no Tizen hardware. This entry rests on user reports and carries no support commitment.
Tizen is not turnkey. There are three install routes and each has a catch.
The released .wgt is unsigned and is for inspection only. Samsung distributor certificates are locked to the DUID of the signer's own panels, so a .wgt we signed would not install on yours.
Native install needs a Samsung certificate tied to each panel's DUID.
The SSSP URL Launcher route works without per-panel signing on your side: the server hosts sssp_config.xml and the panel installs itself, then reinstalls whenever the version bumps.
The simplest route is to point the panel's browser at /player, with no signing at all.
There is no in-app update for this player. A panel keeps its installed build until it is reinstalled.
Requires ScreenTinker 2.0.8 or later. A content security policy added in 2.0.0 black-screened Tizen 5.0 panels and was removed in 2.0.8 (issue #330).

devices.name: LG webOS signage panels
devices.os: webOS 4.x, 5.x and 6.x, and webOS Signage 22 and later
devices.player: webOS .ipk shell around the web player
notes: Community contributed. No LG panel was available to ScreenTinker, so no unit is held in the lab and this carries no support commitment.
Installed from a USB stick or an SI server. No vendor signature is needed.

Built without LG's SCAP library, which LG's licence does not allow us to redistribute. Power control and self-update therefore need a local build with the LG SDK files in place. The dashboard hides those buttons on a panel that reports it cannot do them.
webOS 3.x and older are below the player's baseline and are shown a compatibility message rather than a black screen.

devices.name: Android TV devices (general)
notes: Android TV hardware in general is not certified. Individual models are listed separately when ScreenTinker has tested them.

With group sync enabled the player warms the next clip on a second video decoder shortly before each item boundary. Some chipsets allow only one decoder at higher profiles, and the second request can reclaim the decoder already playing. The picture holds, no error is raised, and the playlist stops advancing.
Reported on Xiaomi Mi TV P1 panels (issue #333) and fixed in 2.0.8. The chipsets that behave this way have never been identified.

devices.name: Amazon Fire TV Stick 4K Select
devices.player: Vega player (vpkg). Played on one AFTCA002, then the process died
notes: Vega OS, not Fire OS. The Android APK does not install. The player is vega/ (see docs/vega-player.md): the web player inside an installed WebView.

Played on one AFTCA002 (ScreenTinker 2.1.6, Kepler 1.2): paired, reported 1920x1080, transitions ran, then the process died in-process. Not certified. Do not buy it for a sign until this entry changes.

Crashes on this stick were a compositor abort, not memory: three died on the same libkepler_slatium stack at a video/image boundary, one with 72 MB of CMA free and no memory stall. Drawing a <video> frame for a transition is what trips it, so video boundaries hard-cut and image transitions stay. CMA pressure is real but survivable — measured falling below 5 MB in 21 of 60 samples, bottoming at 668 kB, with no crash. A 13-minute run across a 44-second image/video cycle was clean.
Group sync does not warm a second video decoder. A second decoder is another CMA claim.
1920x1080 is what that AFTCA002 reported. The stick can output 4K, so this may be the panel or the HDMI link, not a device ceiling.
Offline cache worked on that run: a service worker was in control, images cached, and video decoded offline.
No device-owner kiosk, reboot, RTSP, or package self-update. Back does not quit the app, and that is the whole of the lifecycle control.

devices.name: Amazon Fire TV Stick HD (2026)
devices.player: Vega player (vpkg), not run on this model
notes: Vega OS, not Fire OS. The Android APK does not install. The player is vega/ (see docs/vega-player.md): the web player inside an installed WebView.
Not run on an AFTCL001. The 4K Select run is the only evidence, and that stick is not certified either. Do not buy it for a sign until this entry changes.
Same player as the 4K Select. Transitions are declared. Group sync does not warm a second decoder, because that is a second CMA claim. The earlier browser attempt was not reliable.
1080p is the product's output, not a measurement of this app.
No device-owner kiosk, reboot, RTSP, or package self-update. Back does not quit the app, and that is the whole of the lifecycle control.
